name: Eucalyptus
lede: Eucalyptus is a muted grey-green, named in a 1930 color dictionary for the tree.

sections.title: A 1905 fashion name
sections.body:
The swatch is #A4A07B from Maerz and Paul's *Dictionary of Color* of 1930, which dates the name to 1905, plate 20 C 1 [1]. It is a greyed green, with chroma near 20, nearest to [[sage]] at 8.6 units and to [[light-grape-green]] in the library [1]. Neighbors on a calmer palette are [[sage-green]], [[olive-green]] and [[khaki]] [1].

St Clair records that after 1880 the fashionable partners for heliotrope included canary yellow, eucalyptus green, art bronze and peacock blue [2]. So "eucalyptus green" was already a fashionable shade a generation before Maerz and Paul dated it [1][2].

sections.title: The tree
sections.body:
Authors who mention eucalyptus mostly use it for atmosphere. Finlay notes the smell of the trees in Chile and the pastel green of a clump on pink Australian ground [3][4]. The Pigment Compendium lists two Australian species, *Eucalyptus resinifera* and *E. terminalis*, whose ant-gall residue is red and was traded under the same name as dragon's blood [5]. The artist Concetta Antico, a tetrachromat, painted *Rainbow Eucalyptus* in 2016 [6].

Apart from Finlay's passing 'pastel green' clump, the books say nothing about the color of the leaf, so the link between the swatch and the tree is mostly by name [1][4].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
This muted tone is very common in painting. In our archive of 23,781 paintings, a color within six units of this swatch covers at least five per cent of the canvas in 1,950 works, about 8 per cent [7]. The peak decade is the 1770s, and Impressionism has 21 hits and Post-Impressionism seven, rates only about 1.8 to 1.9 times the archive's [7].

By painter the pattern is sharper: nine of 16 works by Lancret, seven of 13 by Childe Hassam and six of 12 by Willem Roelofs [7]. The strongest single example is *Weizheng Riding on an Ox* by Yamaguchi Sekkei, which has the tone across 87 per cent of the canvas [7]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so a match shows a screen color [7].
